What We Covered:
✅
What is Sorting?
– Arranging data in a logical order (ascending/descending) to make searching, processing, and analysis more efficient.
✅
In-Place vs. Out-of-Place Sorting:
• In-Place Sorting
– Sorts the list without using extra space (e.g., Bubble Sort, Selection Sort).
•
Out-of-Place Sorting
– Requires extra memory to store a new sorted version (e.g., Merge Sort).
✅
Stable vs. Unstable Sorting:
•
Stable Sorting
– Maintains the original order of equal elements (e.g., Bubble Sort).
•
Unstable Sorting
– Does not guarantee original order preservation (e.g., Selection Sort).
✅
Bubble Sort
– Repeatedly swaps adjacent elements until the list is sorted.
✅
Selection Sort
– Finds the smallest element and places it in its correct position, one at a time.

Today, we continued our

🔍 What We Covered:
✅
Insertion Sort
– Builds a sorted list one element at a time, shifting elements as needed.
✅
Counting Sort
– A
distribution-based sorting algorithm
that works well when the range of numbers is small compared to the number of elements.
Faster than comparison-based sorting but requires extra space.
✅
Time Complexity Comparison:
Algorithm
Best Case
|
Average Case
|
Worst Case
🔹Bubble Sort
O(n)
O(n²)

🔹Selection Sort
O(n²)      O(n²)       O(n²)
🔹Insertion Sort
O(n)       O(n²)       O(n²)
🔹Counting Sort
O(n+k)     O(n+k)      O(n+k)
🚀
Which Sort to Use?
• Use Insertion Sort
when the array is
small
or
nearly sorted
.
•
Use Counting Sort
when dealing with a
small range of values
(non-comparative sorting).
•
Bubble Sort and Selection Sort
are generally not the best choices unless for
learning purposes
or
very small inputs
.

🚀 Day 34: Topological Sort
Last weeks lecture was all about
Topological Sorting
—a key algorithm used when solving problems involving dependencies, especially in
Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)
.
📚 What We Covered:
✅ Introduction & Motivation
•
Topological sort arranges tasks so each task appears before those that depend on it.
•
Only possible on DAGs (Directed Acyclic Graphs)—no cycles allowed!
✅ Two Main Implementations:
1. BFS (Kahn’s Algorithm)
•
Starts with nodes having no incoming edges.
•
Removes nodes level by level while tracking dependencies.
•
Efficient and intuitive.
2. DFS-Based Approach
•
Recursively explores paths and builds the order in reverse.
•
Uses a color system (White, Gray, Black) to track cycles.
•
Great for sparse graphs.
✅
Time & Space Complexity:
•
Both BFS and DFS take
O(V + E)
, where
V = vertices
and
E = edges
.
✅
Real-Life Applications:
•
Course scheduling 🏫
•
Task automation 🛠
•
Dependency resolution (e.g., compilers, package managers)
•
Detecting deadlocks 🧠
•
Git commit history & Airflow workflows 🌐
✅
Common Pitfalls:
•
Forgetting to check all components in the graph
•
Cycle detection mistakes using vanilla BFS/DFS
•
Incorrect assumption of node ordering when dependencies exist

Intro to DP
:
Dynamic Programming (DP)
solves complex problems by breaking them into simpler overlapping subproblems and storing their results to avoid redundant work.
Top-down DP =
Recursion

Optimal Substructure
– An optimal solution depends on optimal solutions of its subproblems.
2.
Overlapping Subproblems
– The problem can be broken into smaller, repeated subproblems.

Common DP Applications:

•
Optimizations (e.g. House Robber)

Yes/No decisions (e.g. Partition Equal Subset Sum)
✅
Important Reminders:
•
Always define the state of your subproblem.
•
Have a base case to stop recursion.
•
Watch out for missing parameters when memoizing.

Better memory optimization

dependency order

initial state

Day 41: Tries (Prefix Trees)
Yesterday, we explored
Tries
— a powerful tree-based data structure for efficient string storage and retrieval. 🌳🔡
🧠
What We Covered
✅
What are Tries?
• A tree structure used to store strings where each node represents a character.
• Also called prefix tree or digital tree.
✅
Why Trie?
• Fast prefix and word lookups (like in dictionaries, autocomplete, or spell checkers).
• Saves space when many words share prefixes.
✅
Operations on Tries
•
Insertion
→ add words character by character, marking the end node.
•
Search Prefix
→ check if a given prefix exists by traversing nodes.
•
Search Word
→ same as prefix search, but also check is_end flag.
•
Deletion
→ carefully remove nodes depending on whether the word is unique, prefix of another, or has prefixes itself.
✅
Time & Space Complexity
• Insertion: O(n)
• Search: O(n)
• Deletion: O(n)
(where n = length of word)
• Space: O(M × N) in worst case (M = number of words, N = length of longest word), but often less in practice thanks to shared prefixes.

Day 42: Shortest Path Algorithms
In this session, we explored the core algorithms that power
navigation systems
,
graph optimization
, and
route planning
! 🗺✨
🧠
What We Covered
✅
Dijkstra’s Algorithm
•
Finds the shortest path from a single source to all other nodes in a weighted graph (no negative edges).
•
Uses a min-heap to pick the closest unvisited node.
•
Time Complexity: O((V + E) * logV)
•
Space Complexity: O(V)
✅
Bellman–Ford Algorithm
•
Works even with negative weights.
•
Repeatedly relaxes all edges up to V−1 times.
•
Detects negative weight cycles if a distance decreases after the Vth iteration.
•
Time Complexity: O(V * E)
•
Space Complexity: O(V)
✅
Shortest Path Faster Algorithm (SPFA)
•
An optimization of Bellman–Ford using a queue.
•
Only processes vertices whose distances were updated.
•
Can detect negative cycles using edge count tracking.
•
Average Time: O(E), Worst Case: O(V * E)
•
Space Complexity: O(V)
✅
Floyd–Warshall Algorithm
•
Computes shortest paths between all pairs of nodes.
•
Dynamic programming approach using intermediate nodes.
•
Time Complexity: O(V³)
•
Space Complexity: O(V²)

🚀 Day 43: Advanced String Algorithms
we wrapped up the DSA journey with the fascinating world of
substring search algorithms
, learning how to find patterns efficiently within strings — the foundation of search engines, DNA analysis, and text editors! 🧬✨
🧠 What We Covered
✅
What is a Substring Search? (Naive Method)
• The simplest approach — slide the pattern over the text one by one and compare.
• Time Complexity:
O(n × m)
, where n = length of text and m = length of pattern.
✅
Rabin–Karp Algorithm (Rolling Hash)
• Uses
hashing
to compare substrings efficiently.
• Converts strings to numerical values using polynomial rolling hash.
• Average Time Complexity:
O(n + m)
• Handles substring comparisons with modular arithmetic and base powers.
✅
Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) Algorithm
• Guarantees
O(n + m)
time complexity.
• Avoids re-checking characters by building an LPS (Longest Prefix Suffix) array.
• Two stages:
- Preprocessing: Build the LPS table in O(m).
- Matching: Use LPS to skip unnecessary comparisons in O(n).
✅
Additional String Algorithms
• Z Algorithm: Finds all occurrences of a substring; efficient for multiple pattern matches.
• Manacher’s Algorithm: Finds the longest palindromic substring in O(n).
• Suffix Array: Solves problems related to lexicographic order, substring search, and LCP   (Longest Common Prefix).
